51.author: St. John Chrysostom
51.work: Homilies on the Gospel of St. John, Homily 46
51.text: Chrysostom presses the realism of the gift. The bread the Lord gives is His own flesh; the cup is His own blood. Christ did not soften the saying when many of His disciples found it intolerable. Chrysostom hears in this insistence a fence against every later attempt to read the Eucharist as a memorial only. The bread that came down from heaven is given for the life of the world, and the world receives it as bread, but what it receives is the Lord.

53.author: St. Cyril of Alexandria
53.work: Commentary on the Gospel of John, Book 4
53.text: Cyril makes John 6:53 the keystone of his sacramental theology. The flesh of the Word, having been united to the Word in a single Person, has been quickened by His own life. To receive that flesh is to receive a body charged with the life that conquers death. We are not eating ordinary food and then thinking about Christ; we are receiving the life-bearing Body of the Word, and our own bodies are gathered into the resurrection that has already begun in Him.

53.author: St. Ignatius of Antioch
53.text: Writing on his way to martyrdom around the year 107, Ignatius calls the Eucharist 'the medicine of immortality, the antidote that we should not die but live for ever in Jesus Christ.' Ignatius is the earliest non-canonical witness to the Lord's word in John 6: he ties the eating of the flesh of the Son of Man directly to bodily immortality, well before the formal disputes that would arise centuries later.
